newsitem.title: UK: Concert tunes up as clears first U.S. hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Concert tunes up as clears first U.S. hurdle.

text.p: Concert Plc, the $24 billion planned merger between British Telecommunications Plc and America's MCI Communications Corp, looks set for final approval after clearing its first U.S. regulatory hurdle, analysts said on Tuesday.
BT remained confident of winning definitive clearance from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) by autumn and welcomed Monday's approval of the deal by the Justice Department.

If BT is allowed to buy the 80 percent of MCI it does not already own, it will be granted a place in the history books as having sealed the largest transatlantic merger on record. Few believe the deal will be de-railed so far down the regulatory track.

In comparison to conditions attached to the deal by European regulators two months ago, the U.S. Justice Department (DOJ) waved through the planned merger on Monday asking only for minor assurances on competitive behaviour.
The anti-trust regulator even said the merger would foster competition, citing a 12-cent-per-minute transatlantic telephone call rate initiated by MCI.

"We're pleased that the DOJ has completed its review," a BT spokesman said. "We're optimistic that the DOJ's recommendations on the merger and its competitive benefits will be viewed favourably by the FCC."

BT and MCI want to form a "global supercarrier" that spans the world, offering sophisticated communications services to lucrative, multinational customers. They are in daily contact with regulators and BT said all the signs for final approval looked good.

The DOJ did ask that BT keep secret from MCI any proprietary information it received from other U.S. telecoms carriers. MCI also has to offer rivals room on its existing network to ensure its "gateways" to international traffic do not become bottlenecks.

One analyst noted that in its enthusiasm to win the regulatory green light for the merger, BT would not even view the DOJ's recommendations as an irritant. BT has said it was "only too happy" to agree to two minor concessions already demanded by European regulators.
"These guys are going to agree to anything," noted the telecoms analyst, who declined to be named.
European Union regulators asked that MCI sell its audio-conferencing business in Britain and that it takes further steps to share its undersea cables with rivals.
Concert, a telecoms giant with annual revenues of more than 25 billion pounds ($42.1 billion) and 43 million customers, will be floated in London, New York and Tokyo.
It will be the world's fourth-biggest telecoms group in terms of sales after Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, America's AT&T Corp and Deutsche Telekom AG.
Analysts say the alliance appears to be the best-positioned global carrier in a rapidly consolidating global telecoms industry which is expected to be worth $1.0 trillion by 2000.
Its two rival partnerships are Global One, which links Deutsche Telekom AG, France Telecom and America's Sprint Corp and the Unisource/ World Partners alliances led by AT&T.

Meanwhile, BT's board meets at the end of this month, partly to discuss whether to back down over threats to sue the Labour government over its decision to impose a 500 million pound windfall tax on the group's profits.

Analysts are interpreting what BT has said since last week's budget as a sign that it will not launch a legal challenge -- especially after speculation that the tax could have topped 1.0 billion pounds. ($ = 0.594 British Pounds)
